Number Needed to Treat From a Standardized Mean Difference

Source: R/nnt_from_smd.R
nnt_from_smd.Rd

Converts a standardized mean difference to the success rate difference (SRD) of Kraemer and Kupfer (2006) and to its reciprocal, which they define as the number needed to treat (NNT) for a continuous outcome. The SRD is the probability that a randomly chosen treated person has a better outcome than a randomly chosen control person, minus the probability of the reverse. When sample sizes or confidence limits for the standardized mean difference are given, the function also returns the confidence interval for the SRD and the corresponding confidence set for the NNT, which is two intervals when the interval for the standardized mean difference includes zero.

Usage

nnt_from_smd(
  smd,
  n_1 = NULL,
  n_2 = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  smd_ci_lower = NULL,
  smd_ci_upper = NULL
)

Arguments

smd

The standardized mean difference (Cohen's d): the treatment mean minus the control mean, with higher scores the better outcome, divided by the pooled within-group standard deviation. A single finite number. A negative value gives a negative SRD and a negative NNT, read as the number needed to harm.

n_1, n_2

Sample sizes of the treatment and control groups. Supply both or neither. With both, the noncentral t confidence interval for the population standardized mean difference is computed (ci_smd) and carried to the SRD and the NNT.

conf_level

Confidence level of the noncentral t interval when n_1 and n_2 are given. Default 0.95. With supplied limits, conf_level enters no computation: it is the caller's statement of the level of those limits, and it is recorded and printed only when it is given in the call.

smd_ci_lower, smd_ci_upper

Optional confidence limits for the population standardized mean difference, computed elsewhere. Supply both or neither, with smd_ci_lower not above smd_ci_upper. When supplied they are used as given, the noncentral t computation is skipped, and n_1 and n_2 are not used. An estimate outside its limits is accepted with a warning.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_nnt, a dmar_tbl) with columns term and value. Without an interval the rows are smd, srd (the success rate difference), and nnt. With an interval the rows are, in this order, smd, srd, nnt, smd_ci_lower, smd_ci_upper, nnt_ci_lower, nnt_ci_upper, srd_ci_lower, and srd_ci_upper.

What each row is: smd is the standardized mean difference as given. srd is the success rate difference, \(2 \Phi(d / \sqrt{2}) - 1\). nnt is 1 / srd. smd_ci_lower and smd_ci_upper are the confidence limits for the population standardized mean difference, computed from n_1 and n_2 or as supplied. nnt_ci_lower and nnt_ci_upper are the limits of the NNT when its confidence set is one interval. srd_ci_lower and srd_ci_upper are the limits of the SRD. The result is a dmar_tbl, so tidy(), glance(), and rbind() work on it as on any other. The confidence level is in the conf_level attribute: with n_1 and n_2 it is the level of the computed interval, and with supplied limits it is recorded only when conf_level is given in the call. With an interval the ci_source attribute names smd as the estimate whose interval the others are computed from, so that results_sentence reports the SRD (term = "nnt" or term = "smd" for another) and tidy() gives the confidence level on the rows of the SRD and the NNT and not on those of smd.

srd_ci_lower and srd_ci_upper are the SRD at the two limits of the standardized mean difference and always form an ordinary interval. nnt_ci_lower and nnt_ci_upper depend on where zero falls in the interval for the standardized mean difference:

  • Zero outside the interval: nnt_ci_lower is 1 / srd_ci_upper and nnt_ci_upper is 1 / srd_ci_lower.

  • Lower limit exactly zero: nnt_ci_lower is 1 / srd_ci_upper and nnt_ci_upper is Inf.

  • Upper limit exactly zero and lower limit below zero: nnt_ci_lower is -Inf and nnt_ci_upper is 1 / srd_ci_lower.

  • Zero strictly inside the interval: the confidence set for the NNT is two intervals, which one lower and one upper limit cannot hold, so nnt_ci_lower and nnt_ci_upper are NA. The set is given in the nnt_confidence_set attribute and in a line printed under the table.

In every case, each finite end of the confidence set for the NNT is 1 / srd_ci_lower or 1 / srd_ci_upper.

A result with an interval carries two attributes. nnt_set is "interval" or "two_intervals". nnt_confidence_set is a data.frame with columns lower and upper and one row per interval of the set, in increasing order: one row for "interval", and for "two_intervals" the rows (-Inf, 1 / srd_ci_lower) and (1 / srd_ci_upper, Inf). The two attributes belong to the table itself: tidy() and glance() return the rows without them, so for a set of two intervals they show nnt_ci_lower and nnt_ci_upper as NA; its finite ends are 1 / srd_ci_lower and 1 / srd_ci_upper, which both carry. A table made by rbind() or by taking rows keeps the attributes of the first table, as every dmar_tbl does, so the line printed beneath it describes that table.

The NNT of no effect is infinite: nnt is Inf when smd is zero, and the sign of that infinity has no meaning.

Details

What is estimated. Take one person at random from the treated population and one at random from the control population, with outcomes \(Y_T\) and \(Y_C\), higher being better. The success rate difference is $$\mathrm{SRD} = \Pr(Y_T > Y_C) - \Pr(Y_C > Y_T),$$ the probability that the treated person has the better outcome minus the probability that the control person has, and Kraemer and Kupfer (2006, p. 994) define the number needed to treat for a scaled outcome as its reciprocal, $$\mathrm{NNT} = 1 / \mathrm{SRD}.$$ No response threshold enters: the comparison is between two people, not between each person and a cut. An SRD of 0.25 says that in 100 such pairs the treated person is ahead in about 25 more pairs than the control person is, and the NNT of 4 says that about 4 people must be treated for one more of those comparisons to favor treatment. A negative standardized mean difference gives a negative SRD and a negative NNT, read as the number needed to harm. A standardized mean difference of zero gives an SRD of zero and an infinite NNT (no advantage of either group).

Assumptions, by the part each serves. The point conversion assumes two independent normal populations and a standardized mean difference whose standardizer is the root mean square of the two population standard deviations, which the pooled standard deviation estimates under a common variance (or with equal sample sizes). The interval from n_1 and n_2 assumes normality and a common variance, the conditions of the noncentral t interval for the standardized mean difference (ci_smd; Kelley, 2007). Supplied limits carry whatever assumptions produced them. When the populations are not normal, as with a skewed outcome, a ceiling or a floor, or an ordinal scale, the same standardized mean difference corresponds to a different \(\Pr(Y_T > Y_C)\), and the SRD and the NNT computed here are then answers for a normal model that does not describe the data. How far off they are depends on the two distributions and is not quantified here. cliff_delta estimates the SRD itself from the two samples with no distributional model (Cliff's delta is the sample version of the same difference of probabilities), and vargha_delaney_A estimates \(\Pr(Y_T > Y_C)\), counting half of each tie.

The conversion. Under the normal model the difference \(Y_T - Y_C\) is normal with mean \(d\) and variance 2 in units of the standardizer, so $$\Pr(Y_T > Y_C) = \Phi(d / \sqrt{2}),$$ $$\mathrm{SRD} = 2 \Phi(d / \sqrt{2}) - 1, \qquad \mathrm{NNT} = \frac{1}{2 \Phi(d / \sqrt{2}) - 1}.$$ The function computes the SRD as \(\mathrm{sign}(d) \Pr(\chi^2_1 \le d^2 / 2)\), which is the same number written without the subtraction, so that a standardized mean difference near zero loses no digits to it. The values below agree with Table 1 of Kraemer and Kupfer (2006, p. 992) to the decimals printed there, with one exception: at d = 1.0 the table prints an SRD of .521, and the value is 0.5205, which is 0.520 to three decimals.

The confidence set, and why it can be two intervals. The function starts from a confidence interval for the population standardized mean difference, either the noncentral t interval computed from n_1 and n_2 or the limits supplied. Because the SRD is an increasing function of the standardized mean difference, the SRD at the two limits is a confidence interval for the SRD with the same coverage, and it is always an ordinary interval. The NNT is the reciprocal of the SRD, and the reciprocal is not continuous at zero, so what the interval for the SRD becomes depends on where zero falls:

  • Zero outside the interval. The reciprocal reverses the order of the limits: the interval for the NNT runs from \(1 / \mathrm{SRD}_{\mathrm{upper}}\) to \(1 / \mathrm{SRD}_{\mathrm{lower}}\).

  • Lower limit exactly zero. The interval for the NNT runs from \(1 / \mathrm{SRD}_{\mathrm{upper}}\) to infinity.

  • Upper limit exactly zero and lower limit below zero. The interval runs from minus infinity to \(1 / \mathrm{SRD}_{\mathrm{lower}}\).

  • Zero strictly inside the interval. The SRD values from the lower limit up to zero are sent to the NNT values from \(1 / \mathrm{SRD}_{\mathrm{lower}}\) (negative) down to minus infinity, and the SRD values from zero up to the upper limit are sent to the NNT values from plus infinity down to \(1 / \mathrm{SRD}_{\mathrm{upper}}\). The confidence set is therefore two intervals, \(\mathrm{NNT} \le 1 / \mathrm{SRD}_{\mathrm{lower}}\) (harm) and \(\mathrm{NNT} \ge 1 / \mathrm{SRD}_{\mathrm{upper}}\) (benefit), which meet at infinity, the NNT of no effect (Altman, 1998).

  • No interval requested. Only smd, srd, and nnt are returned.

One lower limit and one upper limit cannot hold a set of two intervals. Reading the two reciprocals as the ends of a single interval would describe the values between them, which are exactly the NNT values the data exclude, and would leave out the NNT of no effect, which the data include. For that case nnt_ci_lower and nnt_ci_upper are therefore NA, the set is in the nnt_confidence_set attribute, and a line under the printed table states it. In every case the confidence set for the NNT is the image of the interval for the standardized mean difference under a one-to-one transformation, so it holds the population NNT exactly when that interval holds the population standardized mean difference, and it has the same coverage. Kraemer and Kupfer (2006) call confidence intervals for the NNT “not advisable” (pp. 992 to 993) and prefer the SRD for interval estimation (p. 994), which is why the limits of the SRD are reported here beside those of the NNT.

Edge cases.

  • smd = 0: the SRD is 0 and nnt is Inf. The sign of that infinity has no meaning.

  • A negative smd: the SRD and the NNT are negative, and with both limits negative the interval for the NNT is an ordered negative interval (for \(d = -0.5\) with 50 per group, \(-17.636\) to \(-2.109\)).

  • A limit exactly zero: one end of the interval for the NNT is infinite, as above; the set is one interval.

  • A very small \(|d|\): the NNT is very large and is computed without loss of digits (for \(d = 10^{-8}\), about \(1.77 \times 10^{8}\)). An SRD that underflows to zero gives an infinite NNT with the sign of \(d\).

  • Very small samples: the noncentral t interval is wide, includes zero for most values of \(d\), and gives two intervals (for \(d = 0.5\) with n_1 = 1 and n_2 = 2, limits for \(d\) of \(-2.07\) and 2.88).

  • An estimate outside the supplied limits is accepted with a warning, and the rows are computed from the three numbers as given.

  • Supplied limits take precedence over n_1 and n_2, which are then neither used nor checked.

  • conf_level must be a single number in (0, 1) even when it enters no computation; NULL is an error.

Which NNT this is. The NNT returned here depends on the standardized mean difference alone. The NNT of evidence based medicine is the reciprocal of a difference between two response proportions at a stated threshold. Under the same normal model, with control response proportion \(p_0\), that NNT is $$1 / \bigl[\Phi\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(p_0) + d\bigr) - p_0\bigr],$$ which changes with \(p_0\) and, for a positive d, is larger than the Kraemer and Kupfer NNT at every threshold. Its smallest value is \(1 / [2 \Phi(d / 2) - 1]\), at \(p_0 = \Phi(-d / 2)\). At \(d = 0.5\) the Kraemer and Kupfer NNT is 3.62; the threshold NNT is at least 5.07 (at \(p_0 = 0.40\)), 5.22 at \(p_0 = 0.5\), and 6.01 at \(p_0 = 0.2\). The two are different quantities and neither is an approximation to the other, so a report should say which one it gives. Furukawa and Leucht (2011) compared the two conversions in individual patient data from antipsychotic trials and found the control event rate conversion closer to the observed NNTs: it fell inside the observed 95 percent interval in 35 of 36 comparisons, against 20 of 36 for the conversion used here. For the NNT at a threshold computed from data, see responder_analysis.

A worked example. nnt_from_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50) returns an SRD of 0.276 and an NNT of 3.62: in 100 pairs of one treated and one control person the treated person is ahead in about 28 more pairs than the control person is, and about 3.6 people must be treated for one more such comparison to favor treatment. The 95 percent limits for the standardized mean difference are 0.101 and 0.897, which exclude zero. The SRD at those limits is 0.057 and 0.474, and the interval for the NNT is their reciprocals in reverse order, 2.11 to 17.64. nnt_from_smd(smd = 0.2, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50) returns an SRD of 0.112 and an NNT of 8.89, with limits for the standardized mean difference of \(-0.193\) and 0.592, which include zero. The interval for the SRD, \(-0.109\) to 0.325, is an ordinary interval and is the one to report. nnt_ci_lower and nnt_ci_upper are NA, and the line under the table gives the confidence set for the NNT as “NNT <= -9.189 (harm) or NNT >= 3.079 (benefit)”: the data are compatible with a benefit as large as one more favorable comparison for every 3.1 people treated, with no effect (an infinite NNT), and with harm as large as one more unfavorable comparison for every 9.2 people treated. A report of this result gives the estimate, 8.89, with both intervals of the set, or gives the SRD with its interval.

References

Altman, D. G. (1998). Confidence intervals for the number needed to treat. BMJ, 317(7168), 1309–1312. doi:10.1136/bmj.317.7168.1309

Furukawa, T. A., & Leucht, S. (2011). How to obtain NNT from Cohen's d: Comparison of two methods. PLoS ONE, 6(4), e19070. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0019070

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. (The noncentral t interval for the standardized mean difference that is carried to the SRD and the NNT here.) doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Kraemer, H. C., & Kupfer, D. J. (2006). Size of treatment effects and their importance to clinical research and practice. Biological Psychiatry, 59(11), 990–996. doi:10.1016/j.biopsych.2005.09.014

See also

smd and ci_smd for the standardized mean difference and its interval; cles for \(\Pr(Y_T > Y_C)\) under the same normal model; cliff_delta and vargha_delaney_A for the same comparisons estimated without the normal model; responder_analysis for the NNT at a threshold.

Examples

# 1. Point estimate only.
nnt_from_smd(smd = 0.5)
#>  term value
#>  smd  0.500
#>  srd  0.276
#>  nnt  3.619

# 2. With the noncentral t interval from the sample sizes.
nnt_from_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50, conf_level = 0.95)
#>  term         value 
#>  smd          0.500 
#>  srd          0.276 
#>  nnt          3.619 
#>  smd_ci_lower 0.101 
#>  smd_ci_upper 0.897 
#>  nnt_ci_lower 2.109 
#>  nnt_ci_upper 17.636
#>  srd_ci_lower 0.057 
#>  srd_ci_upper 0.474 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 3. With limits for the standardized mean difference computed elsewhere.
nnt_from_smd(smd = 0.5, smd_ci_lower = 0.20, smd_ci_upper = 0.80)
#>  term         value
#>  smd          0.500
#>  srd          0.276
#>  nnt          3.619
#>  smd_ci_lower 0.200
#>  smd_ci_upper 0.800
#>  nnt_ci_lower 2.334
#>  nnt_ci_upper 8.892
#>  srd_ci_lower 0.112
#>  srd_ci_upper 0.428

# 4. An interval for the standardized mean difference that includes zero:
#    two intervals for the NNT, printed under the table.
nnt_from_smd(smd = 0.3, smd_ci_lower = -0.10, smd_ci_upper = 0.70)
#>  term         value 
#>  smd          0.300 
#>  srd          0.168 
#>  nnt          5.953 
#>  smd_ci_lower -0.100
#>  smd_ci_upper 0.700 
#>  nnt_ci_lower <NA>  
#>  nnt_ci_upper <NA>  
#>  srd_ci_lower -0.056
#>  srd_ci_upper 0.379 
#> 
#> The interval for the SRD includes 0, so the confidence set for the NNT is two intervals:
#> NNT <= -17.739 (harm) or NNT >= 2.636 (benefit), joined at infinity (Altman, 1998)

# 5. The same case from sample sizes, with the set as an attribute: one
#    row per interval of the set.
res <- nnt_from_smd(smd = 0.2, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50)
res
#>  term         value 
#>  smd          0.200 
#>  srd          0.112 
#>  nnt          8.892 
#>  smd_ci_lower -0.193
#>  smd_ci_upper 0.592 
#>  nnt_ci_lower <NA>  
#>  nnt_ci_upper <NA>  
#>  srd_ci_lower -0.109
#>  srd_ci_upper 0.325 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> The interval for the SRD includes 0, so the confidence set for the NNT is two intervals:
#> NNT <= -9.189 (harm) or NNT >= 3.079 (benefit), joined at infinity (Altman, 1998)
attr(res, "nnt_set")
#> [1] "two_intervals"
attr(res, "nnt_confidence_set")
#>      lower     upper
#> 1     -Inf -9.188745
#> 2 3.079331       Inf

# 6. A negative standardized mean difference: the number needed to harm,
#    with an ordered negative interval.
nnt_from_smd(smd = -0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50)
#>  term         value  
#>  smd          -0.500 
#>  srd          -0.276 
#>  nnt          -3.619 
#>  smd_ci_lower -0.897 
#>  smd_ci_upper -0.101 
#>  nnt_ci_lower -17.636
#>  nnt_ci_upper -2.109 
#>  srd_ci_lower -0.474
